summary: Describes security protocols for SNMP, the authentication and privacy mechanisms used by the party-based SNMP administrative model. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: The secret handshakes and sealed envelopes that network helpers used to prove who they were and keep their messages private.

questions: how does snmp digest authentication work
subtitle: Authentication and encryption protocols for secure network management.

tldr.problem: Network management operations need protection from eavesdropping, message modification, and impersonation. The Simple Network Management Protocol originally lacked strong security mechanisms.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines two security protocols for SNMP: Digest Authentication (using MD5) to verify message integrity and origin, and Symmetric Privacy (using DES encryption) to protect message contents from disclosure.
tldr.outcome: These protocols are now historic, superseded by SNMPv3, which uses more modern security approaches and has largely replaced this party-based model.

today: RFC 1352 defines the party-based SNMP security model and is now Historic. It has been superseded by RFC 3414 (SNMPv3 User-based Security Model), which uses more modern security mechanisms including HMAC for authentication and AES for encryption, and employs a more flexible architecture.

sections.title: Introduction to SNMP Security
sections.content:
The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) is used by network administrators to monitor and manage devices across networks. Because management operations can change critical network settings, SNMP messages must be protected from eavesdropping, alteration, and impersonation. RFC 1352 defines security protocols that work within SNMP's party-based administrative model, where a SNMP party is a virtual execution context with specific permissions and security settings.

The RFC defines protocols to provide three security services: data integrity (ensuring messages are not modified), data origin authentication (verifying the message came from the claimed sender), and data confidentiality (protecting message contents from disclosure). These protocols are secure alternatives to SNMP's trivial protocol, which provides no security whatsoever.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP lets a manager control devices on a network. The security protocols here act like a locked mailbox and tamper-proof seals to keep bad actors from reading or changing management commands.

sections.title: Threats and Security Goals
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several threats specific to network management. The principal threats are modification of information (altering messages to cause unauthorized operations) and masquerade (an attacker assuming another party's identity to issue unauthorized commands). Secondary threats include message stream modification (reordering, delaying or replaying messages) and disclosure (eavesdropping on exchanges).

To counter these threats, the security protocols must verify that messages have not been modified, identify the true originator, ensure messages are recent and ordered correctly, and protect message contents from disclosure. The protocols do not attempt to protect against denial-of-service attacks or traffic analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad actors might try to change commands, pretend to be the manager, replay old commands, or eavesdrop on secrets. The protocols here guard against most of these tricks, but not against simply jamming all messages or watching when commands are sent.

sections.title: Digest Authentication Protocol
sections.content:
The Digest Authentication Protocol provides both integrity and origin authentication using the MD5 message digest algorithm. When a message is sent, a 128-bit digest is computed from the message prefixed with a secret value known only to the sender and recipient. The sender transmits the message along with this digest. The recipient computes the same digest from the received message and secret; if the digests match, the message is authentic and unmodified. If the digests differ, the message has been altered or came from someone without the secret.

Each authenticated message includes a timestamp and a nonce (a unique counter) to prevent replay attacks. The receiving party checks that the timestamp is recent and that the nonce is higher than any previously seen from that sender, ensuring messages are in order and not replayed.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol uses a secret recipe and a fingerprint system. Both the sender and receiver know the secret. The sender makes a fingerprint by mixing the secret into the message and running a formula. The receiver does the same thing; if the fingerprints match, the message is real and unchanged.

sections.title: Symmetric Privacy Protocol
sections.content:
The Symmetric Privacy Protocol encrypts authenticated messages to protect them from disclosure. It uses the Data Encryption Standard (DES) in Cipher Block Chaining mode. The private key for DES is 16 octets: the first 8 octets comprise a 56-bit DES key (with 8 parity bits), and the second 8 octets are the DES initialization vector. Only the originator and recipient know this key; they use it to encrypt and decrypt the message contents.

The protocol requires that any message be authenticated before it can be encrypted. This ensures that confidentiality is layered on top of integrity and origin authentication, providing defense in depth against multiple attack vectors.
sections.plainLanguage: After proving the message is real and unchanged, both sides can scramble the message contents using a secret key only they share. Without the key, an eavesdropper sees only gibberish.

sections.title: Clock Synchronization and Secret Distribution
sections.content:
Both protocols require loosely synchronized clocks between the originator and recipient to prevent replay attacks. The RFC specifies one clock synchronization strategy suited to network management: a responsible management station maintains an authoritative time and periodically synchronizes the clocks of all parties it manages.

Because the protocols depend on shared secret keys, the RFC also defines a secret distribution strategy. Initial configuration must be done manually by a person visiting each device to enter the first secret. A minimal set of three initial parties is recommended: one with no security, one with authentication only, and one with both authentication and privacy. The third party (with both protections) can then securely distribute new secrets to other parties. All secrets must remain known only to authorized software; if a clock is adjusted backward, the secret must be changed to prevent message replay.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides need roughly the same time so they can spot old messages. The network manager has a master clock and syncs all devices. For secrets, someone has to visit each device once to set up the first secret, then that secret is used to safely give the device all the other secrets.
